summary:
EARTHSONA is a browser-based Earth Information Jukebox that makes NASA climate visualizations listenable without disconnecting sound from evidence. In NASA Frames, the app reads six north-to-south latitude stripes from official 2023–2025 NASA Earth Information Center temperature-anomaly maps, turns their rendered red–blue balance into tones in real time, and highlights the stripe being heard. In Climate Globe, it maps 146 annual NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 observations (1880–2025) across latitude bands to one calibrated pitch scale, synchronized with a globe, chart, and source table.

This directly addresses the challenge by pairing an EIC visual frame with a transparent, interactive sonification rather than a pre-rendered soundtrack. Visitors can hear an Arctic–global comparison, then inspect the same NASA values and method. The result is a curious, evidence-led entry point for learners and the public: sound invites pattern discovery, while visible units, controls, and sources keep every note open to questioning.
details:
Try it in one minute

Open NASA Frames and play the 2025 map. Six notes follow the highlighted stripes from north to south. Next, try Listen with Luma and hear the Arctic and global notes for two decades before revealing the numbers.

How a picture becomes sound

The browser samples valid map pixels in six latitude stripes and converts their red–blue balance into pitch. The scan runs in real time on the official 2023, 2024 and 2025 Earth Information Center frames. The resulting sound follows each map’s palette and projection. For a fair temperature comparison across years, switch to Climate Globe.

How a temperature becomes sound

The numeric player maps NASA GISTEMP v4 annual anomalies to a shared scale: 0°C is 220 Hz, and +2°C raises the pitch by an octave within the audio range. Choose any two tracks from eight latitude bands and the published global series, then select a range across 1880–2025. The globe and timeline follow each played year. The data table shows the exact readings behind the notes.

What we found

In the guided test, the same instrument plays the ten-year mean for each series. Between 1980–1989 and 2016–2025, mean anomaly rose from +0.244°C to +2.619°C in the Arctic band (64–90°N), a change of +2.38°C. Globally it rose from +0.247°C to +1.014°C, a change of +0.77°C. Each series uses its own 1951–1980 reference climate. The global mean includes the Arctic, and the result describes these two periods.

Why listen?

A classroom can hear the two pairs before looking at the graph, make a prediction, and then check it against NASA’s table. Keyboard controls, descriptions and exact readings give visitors several ways to explore the same evidence.

How we built and checked it

EARTHSONA uses JavaScript, Canvas, SVG, Web Audio and Vite. The repository pins the NASA CSV and map files, documents both pitch mappings and tests the data import and playback. We cross-checked all 146 annual global values against NASA’s separate global table.
